                      OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY’S RESPONSIVE BRIEF
           I.    Introduction

                 This case presents a straightforward question: Whether the Corporation Commission may

         approve a tariff that permits an independent power producer to furnish electricity directly to a

         large-load consumer within OG&E’s certificated territory, while compelling OG&E to transmit

         and deliver that electricity without purchasing or reselling it. The Legislature has already answered

         that question. Oklahoma law grants certificated retail electric suppliers the exclusive right to

         furnish retail electric service within their assigned territories, subject only to exceptions established

         by statute. See 17 O.S. § 158.25(A). The proponents’ characterization of the arrangement as “self-

         supply” or “wholesale” and the Commission’s ratemaking authority fail to supply any exception

         enacted by the Legislature. Because the proposed arrangements cannot be reconciled with

         Oklahoma law, OG&E respectfully requests that the Commission reject them.

          II.    Background

                 OG&E initiated this proceeding with an Application for an Extra-Large Power & Light

         (“XLPL”) Tariff applicable to new and expanding loads of 75 megawatts or more. Application,

         at 1. The Application responds to Final Order No. 753440 in Case No. PUD 2025-000038 and the

         Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026, which requires separate tariffs and terms

         and conditions for large load customers designed to allocate their costs fairly and secure minimum

         service commitments. 2026 Okla. Sess. Laws ch. 246 (HB 2992), codified at 17 O.S. §§ 901–905.

                 In response, certain parties seek an unbundled service option1 under which large load

         customers ostensibly “self-supply” some or all of their capacity and energy requirements through

         Commission’s ability to approve such relief.” Order No. 761449 (Oct. 21, 2026). Two briefs were

         filed by parties advocating for DODGE proposals—one by Google and a Joint Brief by the Public

         Utility Division (“PUD”) and others.3 The two briefs start from a common template but diverge

         around page 22 of Google’s Brief and page 26 of the Joint Brief. The proponents disagree on

         whether their “BYONG” proposals require unbundling generation and transmission and over how

         to implement and structure their proposed frameworks. Compare Google Br. at 23–28, with Joint

         Br. at 26–39. But both briefs argue that the Commission has authority to order OG&E to handle

         the transmission and distribution for the customer’s preferred third-party supplier. And both briefs

         agree that under their DODGE, the customer would be contracting directly with a third-party

         supplier for the energy that the customer consumes. Yet they call that a “lawful wholesale

         arrangement.” See Joint Br. at 2–5; Google Br. at 1–5.

                 The Attorney General filed a brief advocating a framework called “Accelerated Capacity

         Support” that works within Oklahoma’s “regulated, vertically integrated system and leaves the

         Company as the exclusive retail supplier.” AG’s Br. at 3. OG&E now files this response and, like

         the Attorney General, urges the Commission not to go beyond Oklahoma’s existing law.

         III.    DODGE violates Oklahoma law and neither its proponents’ “wholesale” labels nor
                 retail-wheeling proposals can overcome the Legislature’s commands.

                 The proposed arrangement cannot be reconciled with the statutes governing who may

         furnish retail electric service in Oklahoma. The Legislature granted each certificated supplier

         exclusive retail-service rights, defined retail electric service as selling for ultimate consumption

         rather than simply delivering and billing mechanics and specified the narrow circumstances in



                 3
                  The “Joint Parties” are AARP, the Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers (“OIEC”), Oklahoma
         Sustainability Network (“OSN”), The Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (“PAO”), and PUD. Although
         Google characterizes its submission as a “Joint Brief in Chief” in its opening line, Google is the brief’s sole
         authoring party.
         OG&E Response to Proponents’ Briefs in Chief                                                    Page 5 of 40
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 117 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 40




         which those rights may be displaced. 17 O.S. §§ 158.22(4); 158.25(A) & (F). The proponents’

         own testimony confirms that DODGE would permit an independent producer to furnish electricity

         directly to a consumer while OG&E serves as the delivery conduit. See infra, Section III.A.2.

         Federal law does not transform that retail transaction into a wholesale sale.           Nor can the

         Commission implement the retail-choice restructuring the Legislature considered but never

         authorized. Neither 17 O.S. § 151 nor HB 2992 supplies the missing exception. Each point leads

         to the same conclusion: the Commission cannot approve by tariff what the Legislature has

         prohibited by statute.

                The proponents point to time-of-use rates, interruptible credits, standby service, net

         metering, and economic-development riders. Google Br. at 7; Joint Br. at 8. Every one of those

         mechanisms adjusts the price of retail electric service OG&E alone furnishes. None permit a third

         party to sell the electricity the customer consumes over OG&E’s wires. The two that involve non-

         utility generation prove the point: standby and net-metering service exist for generation on the

         customer’s premises, and the utility’s obligation to interconnect with and purchase from such

         facilities rests on express federal and state authorization. 16 U.S.C. § 824a-3; 17 O.S. §§ 34.1,

         156; OAC 165:40. And when the utility buys a net-metering customer’s excess output, it buys for

         resale, which is exactly the line OG&E draws here. When the Legislature wanted customer

         generation accommodated, it said so and limited that accommodation to on-site facilities. DODGE

         asks for the opposite: remote generation, a third-party seller, and no statutory authority.

                A. The Legislature expressly prohibits third-party retail electric service absent the
                   statutory exception.

                Decades ago, the Legislature unequivocally mandated that retail electric suppliers in

         Oklahoma “shall have the exclusive right to furnish retail electric service to all electric-consuming

         facilities located within its certified territory.” 17 O.S. § 158.25(A) (emphasis added). Equally

         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 117 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 40




         unequivocal is the corresponding prohibition: a retail electric supplier “shall not furnish, make

         available, render or extend [its] retail electric service to a consumer for use in electric-consuming

         facilities located within the certified territory of another electric retail supplier.” Id. (emphasis

         added).

                   Both legislative commands are preceded by the same qualifying phrase: “[e]xcept as

         otherwise provided herein.” Id. That phrase means precisely what it says. And any exceptions to

         the Legislature’s mandates must be found within the statute itself—not fashioned by the

         Commission or devised by parties seeking to circumvent its requirements.

                   After all, only the Legislature, vested with all “Legislative authority of the State,” Okla.

         Const. art. 5, sec. 1, “has the power to change, alter, or amend a statute,” White v. Heng Ly Lim,

         2009 OK 79, ¶ 16, 224 P.3d 679, 685. And just as courts are bound by the Legislature’s

         enactments, so too is this Commission. Indeed, the Oklahoma Constitution provides that the

         Commission’s “authority to prescribe any other rules, regulations or requirements for corporations

         or other persons shall be subject to the superior authority of the Legislature to legislate thereon by

         general laws.” Okla. Const. art. 9, § 18. The Commission’s ratemaking authority cannot alter that

         constitutional hierarchy; even its “paramount” authority to prescribe rates and charges remains

         expressly “subject to regulation by law.” Id. So neither courts nor the Commission may “through

         judicial fiat, change, modify, or amend the expressed intent of the Legislature.” White, 2009 OK

         79, ¶ 16, 224 P.3d at 685. “[T]he wisdom of choices made within the Legislature’s law-making

         sphere are not [the Commission’s] concern, because those choices—absent constitutional or other

         recognized infirmity—rightly lie within the legislative domain.” Head v. McCracken, 2004 OK

         84, ¶ 13, 102 P.3d 670, 680.

                The Legislature thus left no room for ambiguity. The exclusive right is the rule, and the

         Legislature enacted only limited, specific exceptions to it, and the Commission cannot go beyond

         them. Neither does the large-load exception in § 158.25(E) or its related tariff provision in

         subsection (F) authorize a third-party producer to furnish retail service through OG&E’s facilities

         under the proposed DODGE arrangement. Those provisions must be read within the same

         statutory scheme, and neither can suffice to turn a direct-supply arrangement into a wholesale sale

         or to authorize the Commission to dispense with the conditions governing service in another

         supplier’s territory. See Okla. Elec. Coop. v. State ex rel. Okla. Corp. Comm’n, 2025 OK 60, ¶ 14,

         578 P.3d 1201, 1207; Oklahoma Gas & Electric Co. v. Okla. Corp. Comm’n, 2025 OK 43, ¶¶ 10–

         11, 571 P.3d 729, 733–34 (emphasizing that RESCTA exceptions must be read in light of industry

         usage and the broader regulatory scheme).

                DODGE proponents ask the Commission to ignore these cases because they concerned

         RESCTA’s application to “competing retail electric suppliers and the protection of certificated

         service territories.” See Joint Br. at 13; Google Br. at 11. They claim these cases have no

         applicability to their proposed “customer-supported wholesale generation” arrangements, and so

         they conclude no Oklahoma authority addresses their arrangement. Id. That just assumes the

         conclusion. Oklahoma law defines their third-party-sales-for-ultimate-consumption arrangements

         as retail, so these cases are on point. And they underscore that exceptions to the territorial

         framework must be applied according to their statutory terms.

                The large-load exception (1 MW exception) is available only to a retail electric supplier

         extending its own service, and the Supreme Court has construed “extending its service” to mean

         the physical lengthening of the supplier’s existing retail facilities—not reaching a load over

         another entity’s system. Okla. Gas & Elec. Co. v. State ex rel. Okla. Corp. Comm’n, 2025 OK 15,

         Case No. PUD2026-000046

         ¶¶ 37–40, 45–52, 565 P.3d 418, 429–32. An independent power producer has no certified territory,

         no retail facilities to lengthen, and no service to extend. Its only path to the consumer runs through

         OG&E’s system. If a certificated supplier cannot use another’s facilities to reach a large load, an

         uncertificated producer cannot do so under a tariff-sanctioned DODGE proposal. The Supreme

         Court’s reasoning applies equally here:

                 [RESCTA] mandates each respective retail electric supplier to serve every customer
                 in its territory, including the remote, very small, and unprofitable. The Act balances
                 this burden by granting the retail electric supplier an otherwise impermissible
                 monopoly as the only supplier in the territory. To effectively deny the supplier the
                 opportunity to serve the more profitable Large Load customer located within its
                 territory violates the built-in equities of the Act.

         Id. at ¶ 52, 565 P.3d at 432 (emphasis added).4

                 With no statutory language to credibly invoke, proponents of DODGE attempt to redefine

         or ignore the statutory definitions of “retail electric supplier” and “retail electric service” to

         accommodate their desired arrangement and obscure its legal character. See, e.g., Joint Br. at 9–

         10; Google Br. at 8–10. But the Legislature left no uncertainty about the meaning of those terms.5

         Applying those definitions here leads to a single conclusion: any third-party generator under the

         proponents’ proposed arrangements would be a retail electric supplier attempting to furnish, make

         available, render, or extend retail electric service to a consumer for use in an electric-consuming

         facility located within the certified territory of another retail electric supplier—OG&E. That is

         precisely what § 158.25 prohibits.

         station source.”).

                        1. Oklahoma law distinguishes retail service from wholesale energy by
                           consumption and resale.

                Oklahoma law defines “retail electric service” as “electric service furnished to a consumer

         for ultimate consumption,” and contrasts that with “wholesale electric energy,” which is “electric

         energy furnished by an electric supplier to another electric supplier for resale.”            17 O.S.

         § 158.22(4) (emphasis added). The wholesale exception established by the Legislature thus

         contains three essential components: the energy must be (1) furnished by an electric supplier; (2)

         to another electric supplier; and (3) for resale. Id. The statutory test is thus quite simple: A sale

         for consumption is retail, and a sale for resale is wholesale. Id. These are the only attributes that

         matter. If any element is lacking, the wholesale exception does not apply. Under every DODGE

         proposal, there is no logical way to classify the transaction between an unregulated power supplier

         and the XLPL customer as wholesale consistent with the statutory definition. The contemplated

         transactions are all retail and thus not permitted by law.

                Tellingly, while both briefs claim that “[e]very attribute that defines retail electric service

         remains with the incumbent,” see Joint Br. at 5; Google Br. at 4, they fail to acknowledge the key

         element of a “resale” as the only statutory attribute the Legislature proscribed to distinguish

         wholesale sale from “retail electric service”, compare Joint Br. at 5; Google Br. at 4 (describing

         delivery-related services), with 17 O.S. § 158.22(4) (making the defining attribute of “retail

         electric service” the furnishing of electricity “for ultimate consumption” as opposed to furnishing

         of electricity “to another electric supplier for resale”); cf. 16 U.S.C. § 824(d) (defining “wholesale”

         as the “sale of electric energy to any person for resale” (emphasis added)).

                Proponent’s point to how their DODGE proposals would have OG&E still conducting

         some of the aspects of retail electric service. See Joint Br. at 4–5; Google Br. at 4–5. But the

         statutory test does not look to these attributes. Within Oklahoma’s bundled retail electric system,


         OG&E Response to Proponents’ Briefs in Chief                                            Page 10 of 40
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 117 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 40




         these functions—transmission, delivery, etc.—always accompany retail electric service, but they

         do not create any distinctions that are relevant to the statutory interpretation question of whether

         DODGE transactions are retail sales. Oklahoma law draws the line between retail and wholesale

         at whether the product is being sold for consumption or resale. 17 O.S. § 158.22(4). It is irrelevant

         whether OG&E delivers the third-party supplier’s electricity or handles the billing for the retail

         electricity the supplier wheels through OG&E’s infrastructure to the end user. The dispositive

         question is whether the independent producer is selling the electricity for resale by the customer.

         See 17 O.S. § 158.22(4). As the proponents describe DODGE, they will not; the customer will not

         be reselling anything.

                 The DODGE proponents claim that “[n]othing in RESCTA conditions a utility’s

         certificated retail supplier status on the utility generating or procuring one hundred percent of the

         energy.” See Joint Br. at 9; Google Br. at 8. That ignores the broader context of Oklahoma’s

         integrated electric utility framework. RESCTA makes no distinction between generation and

         transmission when it defines “retail electric service” as “electric service furnished to a consumer

         for ultimate consumption.” 17 O.S. § 158.22(4). Within Oklahoma’s bundled utility framework,

         electric service includes generation, transmission, and delivery of electricity for ultimate

         consumption. See id.; see also infra, Section III.D. After all, public utilities include entities

         involved in furnishing “the production, transmission, delivery, or furnishing of electric current for

         light, heat, or power.” 17 O.S. § 151(A)(1)(c). Whether a retail electric supplier generates the

         electricity it sells or procures it from another electric supplier, it is still a retail electric supplier if

         it furnishes electric service to a customer for ultimate consumption. 17 O.S. § 158.22(4). So

         contrary to proponent’s arguments, RESCTA does indeed condition an electric utility’s retail status

         on whether it sells electric service (regardless of how it acquires the electricity) to end users. Id.

         § 158.22(1) & (4).

                 Proponents repeatedly describe the transactions they seek to authorize in terms that are

         indistinguishable from retail sales. Google describes the arrangement as one in which the customer

         procures the generation necessary to serve its own load from third-party resources. Google Br. at

         4. The Joint Parties do the same. Joint Br. at 4. Indeed, both briefs acknowledge that the

         arrangement concerns “a customer’s procurement of the commodity it consumes.” Google Br. at

         11 (emphasis added); Joint Br. at 13. And both briefs recognize that the electricity consumed by

         the customer may be procured under a contract OG&E never signed and is not privy to. Google

         Br. at 20; Joint Br. at 23. Yet still they call these “wholesale” transactions to get around RESCTA.

                 Simply labeling the arrangement a wholesale transaction does not make it one.6 Just as a

         rose by any other name is still a rose, a sale for ultimate consumption by any other name is still a

         retail sale. See WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE, ROMEO AND JULIET act 2, sc. 2; 17 O.S. § 158.22(4).

                         2. The proponents’ own testimony and briefing confirms that DODGE
                            furnishes electricity for ultimate consumption, not resale.

                 The proponents’ own testimony confirms that DODGE falls on the retail side of the

         statutory line. Google describes “self-supply” as an arrangement in which “a large-load customer

         takes direct financial and contractual responsibility for securing the generation resources needed

         to serve its electricity demand, while OG&E continues to provide regulated retail delivery service.”



                 6
                   The proponents cannot settle on what their own transaction is. Sometimes the customer procures
         “the commodity it consumes” from a third party, Google Br. at 11; Joint Br. at 13; other times the generator
         merely sells into SPP while OG&E serves “its retail customer’s entire load,” Google Br. at 20; Joint Br. at
         23. Either way, DODGE fails. In the first version, the third party is furnishing retail electric service in
         OG&E’s territory, which § 158.25(A) forbids. In the second, OG&E is the only retail supplier, the third-
         party generator sells to the market rather than the customer, and the customer’s side agreement is at most a
         financial hedge, Joint Br. at 25, which supplies no basis for zeroing out charges for generation service
         OG&E actually provides. The result is either unlawful retail competition or an unlawful cost shift.
         OG&E Response to Proponents’ Briefs in Chief                                                Page 12 of 40
         Case No. PUD2026-000046

         Kimbrough Responsive Test. at 52:9–13. More specifically, “the customer enters into a long-term

         PPA with an independent power producer” and “a customer procures and pays an independent

         power producer for 100 percent of its accredited generation capacity and energy.” Id. at 51:14–

         20; 55:21–23, 56:1. The customer thus obtains and pays directly for generation from the third

         party to serve its own electricity demand—ultimate consumption—while OG&E provides the

         forced delivery service.

                Google proposes that OG&E “continue[] to provide local delivery, metering, retail billing,

         scheduling, and market settlement services” but “[c]rucially . . . OG&E does not procure or

         construct the generation capacity” supplied through the arrangement. Id. at 52:21–22, 53:1–3.

         Likewise, the purported “self-supplying customer remains fully responsible for its generation

         supply costs while continuing to pay all Commission-approved delivery, transmission, metering,

         and administrative charges to OG&E.” Id. at 56:10–13. Summing it up, Kimbrough says, “The

         customer pays OG&E for every dollar of transmission, delivery, and administrative service it uses,

         but does not pay OG&E for utility generation capacity that the customer has independently

         financed” and received from a third party. Id. at 58:7–10. In other words, OG&E is not reselling

         electricity to the customer.

                OG&E witness Kimber L. Shoop confirms those mechanics. As he explains, under the

         proposed arrangement, “the host utility is not a party to the underlying bilateral CPA between the

         large customer and the third-party generator.” Shoop Rebuttal Test. at 20:24–27. Rather, the

         customer selects the resource and negotiates its terms, while the utility “pays $0.00 to the generator

         for the power and assesses $0.00 per kW and $0.00 per kWh to the customer on its retail bill for

         that generation.” Id. at 21:3–4. OG&E instead “functions exclusively as a delivery conduit and

         scheduling agent, never acquiring legal ownership of the power.” Id. at 21:5–6. Thus, even apart
